task_1.title: Enable autoescaping by default for SVG templates
task_1.description: Flask 2.2.3 changes default template autoescaping so `.svg` templates are escaped the same way as HTML and XML templates. Rendering SVG templates with dynamic text should now escape special characters automatically instead of requiring a workaround such as renaming the template or overriding autoescape behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that SVG template files are autoescaped by default so dynamic content inserted into rendered SVG output is safely escaped and behaves consistently with other markup template types.

expectation.grounded: Flask's default autoescape selection must treat template names ending in `.svg` as autoescaped, alongside `.html`, `.htm`, `.xml`, and `.xhtml`. Calls that render SVG templates through the standard template rendering flow should therefore escape inserted text by default when no explicit autoescape override is provided.
expectation.conceptual: Applications rendering SVG templates should get the same default escaping behavior they already expect for other markup templates. Dynamic values containing markup-sensitive characters should render safely in SVG output without extra configuration.

constraints.grounded: The default behavior for existing autoescaped template extensions must remain unchanged, the no-template-name case must still default to autoescape enabled, and this update should only change the default classification of `.svg` templates rather than requiring callers to change rendering APIs.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade should add SVG to the existing safe default behavior without regressing current escaping behavior for other template types or changing how applications invoke template rendering.

behavior: A template whose name ends with `.svg` is now considered autoescaped by default.
Rendering an SVG template with dynamic text escapes special characters in the output unless the application explicitly disables or overrides autoescaping.
SVG templates now behave consistently with HTML and XML template types under Flask's default template autoescape rules.
acceptance_criteria: When an application renders a `.svg` template through Flask's standard template rendering flow, it should autoescape injected values by default.

When a value rendered into an SVG template contains markup-sensitive characters such as an ampersand or angle brackets, the resulting SVG output should contain escaped text rather than raw characters.
When rendering templates with existing autoescaped extensions such as `.html`, `.htm`, `.xml`, or `.xhtml`, their default autoescaping behavior should remain unchanged.
When Flask determines autoescape behavior without a template filename, it should continue to default to autoescaping enabled.

task_2.title: Type template_folder as path-like
task_2.description: Version 2.2.3 updates the public typing contract for template folder configuration so Flask and Blueprint constructors formally accept pathlib.Path and other os.PathLike values for template_folder, aligning that parameter with existing path-like support patterns and removing type-checking friction for valid usage.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications and blueprints can provide template folder locations as either strings or path-like objects, so valid pathlib.Path usage is recognized as supported by the public API.

expectation.grounded: The public constructor signatures for Flask, Blueprint, and the shared Scaffold base should define template_folder as an optional union of str and os.PathLike rather than only str. Passing a pathlib.Path as template_folder should therefore be treated as supported API usage and should align with the typing already exposed for static_folder.
expectation.conceptual: Template folder configuration should accept both plain string paths and modern path objects. Developers using pathlib.Path for template directories should be able to do so without the framework API signaling that the value is invalid.

constraints.grounded: This change is limited to the public typing and supported API contract for template_folder. Existing string-based usage must remain valid, the parameter must remain optional, and the default Flask template folder behavior must remain unchanged.
constraints.conceptual: The update should broaden accepted template path representations without changing existing behavior for current users or altering default template lookup configuration.

behavior: Flask should expose template_folder as an optional path-like parameter that accepts either str or os.PathLike values.
Blueprint should expose template_folder as an optional path-like parameter that accepts either str or os.PathLike values.
The shared scaffold-level API contract should consistently reflect path-like support for template_folder so derived framework objects present the same accepted parameter types.
Using pathlib.Path for template_folder should be considered supported usage by type-aware tooling and API consumers.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer constructs a Flask application with template_folder set to a pathlib.Path, the public API contract should treat that argument type as valid.
When a developer constructs a Blueprint with template_folder set to a pathlib.Path, the public API contract should treat that argument type as valid.
When template_folder is omitted or provided as a string, behavior and supported usage should remain unchanged.
The accepted type for template_folder should be consistent with the framework's existing path-like support model for comparable folder path parameters.

task_3.title: Restore `flask run --debug` support
task_3.description: Flask 2.2.3 fixes the `flask run` command so its documented `--debug` option is actually supported. Users can invoke debug mode directly from the run command, and the command-line help now matches real behavior instead of advertising an unusable flag.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the `flask run` command supports the documented `--debug` option so users can start the development server in debug mode without the command being rejected.

expectation.grounded: The `flask run` CLI command must expose a `--debug` option and accept it during argument parsing. When `--debug` is provided to `flask run`, the command should activate Flask's documented debug-mode run behavior, including debugger and reloader behavior associated with that option, instead of treating the flag as unsupported.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to enable debug mode directly on `flask run` with the documented flag. The help text and the actual command behavior should agree.

constraints.grounded: This update should only close the gap between the documented `flask run` interface and its actual accepted options. Existing `flask run` behavior without `--debug` should remain intact, and the `--debug` flag should follow Flask's existing debug-mode semantics rather than introducing a separate workflow.
constraints.conceptual: Do not change the normal startup path for users who do not opt into debug mode. The fix should make the advertised flag usable and consistent, not redefine how the server runs.

behavior: `flask run` now recognizes `--debug` as a valid command option.
Running `flask run --debug` no longer fails because the option is unrecognized or unsupported.
Supplying `--debug` to `flask run` enables the command's debug-mode server behavior, including debugger and reload support described for that flag.
The supported options for `flask run` are now consistent with its documented help output.
acceptance_criteria: When a user runs `flask run --debug`, the command should be accepted and proceed with debug-mode startup instead of failing during CLI option parsing.
When a user views `flask run --help`, `--debug` should be presented as a supported option for that command.
When a user runs `flask run` without `--debug`, the existing non-debug invocation path should remain available.
When a user chooses `--debug`, the observable development-server behavior should match Flask's documented debug-mode behavior for that option.
